hook: Alcohol doesn't help you sleep. It sedates you — and sedation and sleep are neurologically completely different states.
topic: Alcohol as REM suppressor — perception vs. architecture
body:
**Alcohol is the most commonly used sleep aid on the planet. It works — in the narrow sense that it reduces the time it takes to lose consciousness. The problem is that unconsciousness and sleep are not the same thing.**

Alcohol is a GABA-A receptor agonist. It produces sedation through a mechanism that is fundamentally different from natural sleep onset. Under alcohol, your brain is sedated — not cycling through the structured stages that make sleep restorative.

Specifically: alcohol is a potent suppressor of REM sleep. In the first half of the night, alcohol metabolises and its sedative effect allows some slow-wave sleep to occur. But as blood alcohol clears in the second half of the night, the brain rebounds — entering a hyperaroused state. This is when REM is displaced, sleep becomes fragmented, and the 3am wake becomes more likely.

The result is a night that felt better than it was. You don't remember the fragmentation. You remember falling asleep quickly. So the association between alcohol and sleep feels real — even though the architecture was systematically disrupted.

The night you drink, you sleep. You just don't restore. That distinction costs more than most people realise.

Full breakdown in the guide — link in bio.
